A1.justification: Both PDFs describe successive versions of the same exploration work despite retitling HyperAgent as Ensemble++. Matching algorithms, theoretical arguments, and retained experimental plots establish continuity. Both PDFs, including their appendices, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original linear and nonlinear bandit simulations and content-moderation experiments in Section 4 and Appendix F.

after.justification: V3 reports original benchmark, computational-cost, and ablation results in Section 6 and Appendices B and I, alongside retained experiments.

M1.justification: V3 introduces stop-gradient in the uncertainty branch, preventing uncertainty-head gradients from updating shared features, and formulates symmetrized, decoupled neural training in Section 4 and Appendix C. This substantively changes the shared-feature training procedure described in v1. Random linear index sampling and the core linear incremental updates already existed.

E1.justification: V3 adds classification bandits using UCI Mushroom and Shuttle and a vector-quadratic reward environment (Section 6, Appendix I.2). The earlier linear, neural, quadratic, and hate-speech tasks remain represented. These additions substantially broaden evaluation beyond the earlier synthetic and language tasks.

E2.justification: Greedy is removed from the hate-speech comparison (v1 Figure 7 versus v3 Figure 3). V3 Figure 1 includes original-schedule LMCTS in the joint quadratic comparison, whereas v1 evaluated that variant separately in Figure 16. Ensemble+, EpiNet, and LMCTS remain established comparators.

E3.justification: The neural/quadratic comparisons change from five-million-step runs in v1 to 100,000-step curves in v3, with Coord replacing Sphere as the default update distribution. V3 Appendix I.2 specifies sampling 50 of 1,000 actions each round. V3 also adds wall-clock time per step as an evaluation metric and drops the Pythia14M configuration.

E4.justification: V3 adds shared-versus-independent ensemble diagnostics, shared-layer hyperparameter sweeps, stop-gradient and symmetry ablations, and nonlinear ensemble-size and buffer-size studies (Figures 2, 4, 7–8, and 18). Earlier pretraining, frozen-versus-fine-tuned backbone, and update-sample-count analyses disappear. Existing linear distribution analyses are largely retained.

E5.justification: V1 Appendix F.2 reports ten distinct random seeds for nonlinear experiments; v3 Appendix I.2 reports five. Linear experiments retain 200 repetitions. Both versions display variability, without introducing a new significance-testing or confidence-interval procedure.

E6.justification: V3 adds UCI and vector-quadratic benchmark outcomes, measured runtime curves, and findings such as linear regret when stop-gradient is removed (Figures 1, 4, and 16). Earlier GPT/Pythia fine-tuning and pretraining results are removed. Linear heatmaps are retained unchanged. Revised neural curves use changed conditions and do not establish same-setting gains over v1.

T1.justification: V3 adds RLS posterior-matching and gradient derivations and revises Lemma 1's probability accounting and ensemble-size threshold. Its main regret theorem also changes substantively: v1 Theorem 2 uses a time-dependent confidence factor and an additional regret term; v3 Theorem 1 omits them, although Appendix F.2 retains the log-determinant confidence factor and martingale argument. Much of the original covariance and anti-concentration analysis survives.

C1.justification: V1 centers on integrating existing HyperAgent with foundation models for uncertainty-aware online decisions. V3 instead presents Ensemble++ as a novel solution to ensemble coupling through gradient decoupling, symmetrization, and continuous sampling. Foundation-model moderation becomes one application within a broader ensemble-exploration contribution. The headline scalability and Thompson-sampling regret claims remain.

C2.justification: V3 adds a substantial mechanism account linking shared-layer gradient interference, homogenization, and sequential dependency to ineffective exploration, with stop-gradient and symmetry presented as remedies. Appendix J adds architecture-based explanations of computational differences from EpiNet. The earlier limitation concerning ensemble-size dependence in the regret bound is retained in Appendix I.1.

D1.justification: V3 supplies substantially more implementation guidance: ensemble size 8, buffer size 50,000, two-layer 64-unit MLP backbones, neural prior details, sampling pseudocode, and baseline implementation sources. Its reproducibility statement specifies CPUs for linear experiments and V100 GPUs for GPT-2, refining v1's blanket P40 report. The advertised code repository also changes.

R1.justification: Research positioning shifts from foundation agents and hypermodels toward ensemble coupling, RLS, and perturbed-history exploration. V3 adds works including Osband and Van Roy (2015), Lu and Van Roy (2017), Papandreou and Yuille (2010), and Kveton's bandit studies. Broad foundation-model coverage, including Gemini and Voyager citations, is removed. This exceeds bibliographic updating.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. V3 adds dedicated background and ensemble-coupling sections, reorganizes the appendices, and moves the general regret framework and much of the moderation motivation out of the main narrative. The title, terminology, authorship, and document organization also change.

P2.justification: V3 replaces the GPT-specific architecture sketch with comparative shared-layer and Ensemble++ diagrams, adds runtime and diagnostic plots, introduces comparison and summary tables, and regroups experimental displays. The moderation pipeline and retained linear plots move to different locations. A new document layout and appendix contents pages substantially change presentation.

improvement.justification: V3 provides broader empirical coverage, useful mechanism ablations, and substantially better implementation documentation. However, its central regret statement becomes inconsistent with its appendix: Theorem 1 drops the log-determinant confidence growth used in v1 Theorem 2, while Appendix F.2 retains it. This unresolved theoretical discrepancy materially offsets the empirical and documentation benefits, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
